General Conclusion


<!-- Page 79 -->


71

This dissertation sought to grapple with fundamental questions related to safety,

prediction, and intervention in the emerging field of real-time monitoring research for STBs. The

first paper experimentally examined the effects of frequent assessment on the severity of suicidal

thinking and found no iatrogenic effects. The second paper examined the generality of a

prominent theory of suicide and found a lack of universal effects and overall heterogeneity in

effects. The third paper tested a real-time barrier reduction intervention tool to promote the use

of crisis resources and found high engagement with the tool and low use of crisis resources. In

this concluding section of this dissertation, I describe what was learned from these three papers

and crucial directions for future research.

The first paper dealt with the safety of real-time monitoring. This paper specifically

focused on the effects of assessment on the real-time severity of suicidal thinking. Given the

growing number of real-time monitoring studies of STBs, this is a fundamental and crucial

question. While there had been numerous observation papers on the effects of real-time

assessment (Husky et al., 2014), there were several important advances with this paper. The first

was the use of an experimental design (i.e., the manipulation of the number of surveys per day)

rather than merely examining observational long-term temporal trends in the data. This type of

experimental manipulation had been used in limited ways in prior research (Law et al., 2015).

The experimental approach provides greater confidence in causal inference. The second was the

examination of effects over shorter timescales (e.g., minutes) than in prior research. This

provides greater precision in understanding if and when effects could occur. What was learned

from this study was that on average there does not seem to be evidence of iatrogenic effects of

real-time assessments on the real-time severity of suicidal thinking.


<!-- Page 80 -->


72

Since the publication of this paper, several other papers have replicated the finding that

real-time assessments of suicidal thinking do not appear to iatrogenic and is acceptable in various

populations (Glenn et al., 2022; L. M. M. Kivelä et al., 2023; Rogers, 2021). There are several

important directions for future research in this area. The first is examining potential individual

differences in reactivity to assessment. It is quite possible that real-time assessments may be

more acceptable and less stressful for some participants than others. Preliminary research

suggests that while individuals do not differ in real-time data reactivity effects, they may

retrospectively report differences in their overall experiences completing the real-time surveys

(L. M. M. Kivelä et al., 2023). One way to gain better insight into these potential individual

differences would be using qualitative data (Rogers, 2021) and interviews at the end of studies to

better understand participants’ experiences in this type of research. This type of data may allow

future research to optimize protocols to reduce participant burden. Finally, while a growing body

of research including this paper suggests it is safe and feasible to collect real-time data on STBs,

compliance and missing data in real-time protocols remains a crucial issue (Ammerman & Law,

2022; Wrzus & Neubauer, 2022). More in-depth examinations of predictors of compliance

(Jacobucci et al., 2023) improving the design of real-time studies to reduce missing data is an

important next step to increase the usefulness of this research.

The second paper of this dissertation focused on the real-time prediction of suicidal

thinking and generality of risk factors. This paper represents a new direction in suicide prediction

research. Rather than examining prediction across people, this paper examined prediction within-

people over time (Sewall & Wright, 2021). To bridge into this new world of prediction and

individual modeling of longitudinal data, I used factors from a prominent existing theory of

suicide (T. Joiner, 2007). Rather than finding support factors that generalized across all


<!-- Page 81 -->


73

participants, we found heterogeneity in individual models. No psychological risk factor appeared

across all participants in either of the sample. Other published studies using this approach to

examining real-time suicide risk have also found heterogeneity rather than generality (Kaurin et

al., 2021; Yin et al., 2023). This study and other work suggest heterogeneity in suicide risk and

the need to consider heterogeneity when developing useful assessments, prediction models, and

interventions.

There are several important future areas of research regarding heterogeneity in STBs and

individual level modeling of risk. First, this study only considered heterogeneity in risk factors

for suicidal thoughts. Heterogeneity, however, could manifest in several other ways. For

example, there could be heterogeneity in the frequency of suicidal thoughts (Kleiman et al.,

2018) or the content of suicidal thinking (Miranda et al., 2023). Second, this study focused on

improved model fit for prediction (Lane et al., 2019) rather than machine learning based

prediction accuracy of real-time suicidal thinking severity scores. An important future area of

research for increasing the usefulness of individual statistical models is to test the accuracy of

these models for predicting STB outcomes (Barrigon et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2023; S. Wang et al.,

2023). Finally, to increase the clinical utility of individual models, more work is needed to

understand how both participants and clinicians understand and use the results of these models

(Frumkin et al., 2021). Along those lines an important step in any type of clinical translation is

understanding the minimum amount of real-time data is needed to generate stable individual

models of risk (Hoekstra et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023). An individual approach to suicide risk

holds great promise, but much more work is needed to refine this approach for better precision

and clinical utility.


<!-- Page 82 -->


74

The third paper of this dissertation focused on adapting and then testing a barrier-

reduction intervention that promotes the use of crisis resources in the context of real-time

monitoring research. I was able to successfully adapt, build out this real-time tool (ResourceBot),

and then test it among a sample of adults with recent suicidal thoughts. One thing that was

learned from this paper is that this type of approach has high feasibility with the tool being

deployed frequently and there being high engagement with the tool. There was less strong

support for acceptability with moderate retrospective acceptability ratings of the tool and low

uptake of resources in the study. The study also provided rich insights into the concerns

participants have about crisis resources (e.g., that they won’t help) and the types of resources

they are most interested in (e.g., text-based crisis lines). Given the growing role of crisis lines in

mental health care (Zabelski et al., 2023) and research safety protocols, this paper highlights the

need for more research into attitudes towards them and use of them.

I view the third paper as a first step in developing effective, safe, and scalable real-time

interventions for suicide risk that can be built upon in future research. First, a significant

limitation of the paper was the simple nature of the tool and limited scope of the type of

resources offered. In future work, a broader battery of resources or skills could be offered to

participants in this type of real-time tool. This could either be a general battery of skills and

resources or they could be more personalized. For example, at baseline when participants are not

distressed, they could select from a broader battery the three resources or skills that would find

most helpful when in distress. Then during the real-time monitoring period only those resources

or skills would be available for that participant. Second, another limitation was simple decision

rule to trigger the deployment of the tool. In future research, more dynamic, complex, or

personalized decision rules may increase receptivity and engagement with the tool (Künzler et


<!-- Page 83 -->


75

al., 2019). Finally, participants may have developed their own skills or resources for coping with

suicidal thoughts (Stanley et al., 2021). Better understanding how people already cope with their

own suicidal thinking may be one pathway towards building more effective real-time

interventions.

Real-time monitoring research for STBs is a new, but quickly growing area of research

(Kleiman et al., 2023). Much has been written about the promise of using these technologies to

advance suicide research and prevention (Allen et al., 2019; Coppersmith et al., 2022; Kleiman

& Nock, 2018; Millner et al., 2020). This dissertation highlights overall that it is feasible to use

technologies, such as smartphones, to attempt to understand, predict, and help prevent STBs.

This dissertation also displays the many ethical, statistical, and logistical challenges in realizing

the potential of these technologies. Given the immense complexity of suicide and the challenges

of suicide prevention, it is unlikely these technologies will be a panacea. Through continued

systematic and thoughtful inquiry, however, this research could provide new clinical insights and

these technologies could one day help prevent suicide.
